31.quote_or_event: “Religion is supremely auspicious; non-violence, selfcontrol and penance are its essentials. Even the gods bow down before him whose mind is ever preoccupied with religion.”
31.explanation: The Dasavaikalika Sutra opens by declaring dharma, made up of non-injury, restraint and austerity, the highest good (mangala), and says even celestial beings honour the person whose mind rests always in it.
31.tie_back: Like the Kural's opening question, 'what greater good than virtue?', this text places dharma above every other good and says it wins the highest honour. The Kural adds wealth to the list of virtue's rewards; the Jain verse does not.
31.source: Dasavaikalika Sutra 1.1, as Saman Suttam v. 82, Dharmasutra (tr. T.K. Tukol and K.K. Dixit; text via jainworld.com)
31._accuracy_note: Verified on jainworld's Saman Suttam page (its typo 'p[enance' read as 'penance'); a strong match on virtue as the supreme good and source of honour, but Jainism treats worldly prosperity as at most a by-product of merit (punya), not one of dharma's goals as the Kural's 'selvam' implies.

32.quote_or_event: “As the fallow leaf of the tree falls to the ground, when its days are gone, even so the life of men (will come to its close); Gautama, be careful all the while!” … “Thus the soul which suffers for its carelessness, is driven about in the Samsara by its good and bad Karman”
32.explanation: In the 'Leaf of the Tree' lecture Mahavira warns his chief disciple Gautama, in a refrain repeated throughout, never to lapse into carelessness (pramada) even for a moment, because heedlessness is what keeps the soul drifting through rebirths.
32.tie_back: The Kural places the worst ruin not in active vice but in forgetting virtue. Jainism likewise names inattentive carelessness, pramada, as the root of the soul's undoing.
32.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 10.1 and 10.15 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895)
32._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim (diacritics simplified in 'Samsara'); pramada as heedless forgetting closely matches Parimelazhagar's reading of 'marathal' as delusion rather than defiance, though the text has no explicit gain-versus-ruin contrast.

33.quote_or_event: Umasvati's Tattvartha Sutra defines yoga as the activity of body, speech and mind, says this activity is the channel through which karma flows into the soul (asrava), and teaches that wholesome activity is the cause of merit (punya) while unwholesome activity is the cause of demerit (papa).
33.explanation: In Jain doctrine, every movement of mind, speech and body draws karmic matter to the soul. The layperson is therefore asked to make each of these three channels wholesome, as far as their capacity allows, while the monk aims to restrain them altogether.
33.tie_back: Parimelazhagar glosses the Kural's 'every place good can reach' as the three instruments of mind, speech and body. These are exactly Jainism's three yogas, which must be kept wholesome without letting up.
33.source: Tattvartha Sutra 6.1-3 (Umasvati; cf. tr. Nathmal Tatia, That Which Is, 1994)
33._accuracy_note: The mind-speech-body triad matches the commentarial gloss exactly, but this is paraphrase rather than a verified quotation, and Jainism holds that even wholesome activity binds karma (as merit), so it does not share the Kural's unqualified call to ceaseless doing.

34.quote_or_event: Near the end of the Samayasara, Kundakunda says that deluded people take up the many outward marks (linga) of monks or of householders and call them the path to liberation. No outward mark is that path, he says: the Jinas teach that the path is right faith, right knowledge and right conduct within the soul.
34.explanation: Kundakunda, the most influential Digambara teacher, insists that a monk's robes or nakedness, a householder's observances and any other outward sign of religion count for nothing in themselves. Only the inner purity of the soul is the way to release.
34.tie_back: The Kural says that a mind free of stain is the whole of virtue and that everything else is mere noise and show, and Parimelazhagar names outward religious garb (vedam) as part of that show. Kundakunda makes the same move, refusing to let outward marks stand in for inner purity.
34.source: Samayasara of Kundakunda, gathas on linga, c. 408-411 (numbering per Amritachandra's recension; varies between editions)
34._accuracy_note: A strong and distinctly Jain match, including the commentators' point about garb, but I could not find an online English translation to check wording or exact gatha numbers, so this is paraphrase with approximate numbering.

35.quote_or_event: “Anger destroys love, pride destroys modesty, deceit destroys friendship; greed is destructive of everything.” … “One ought to put an end to anger through calmness, pride by modesty, deceit by straight-forwardness and greed by contentment.”
35.explanation: Jain ethics names four passions (kashaya), anger, pride, deceit and greed, as the fundamental stains that bind karma to the soul. The Dasavaikalika says what each one destroys and which virtue overcomes it.
35.tie_back: The Kural defines virtue as conduct that steadily avoids four named faults. Jainism likewise defines purity through a fixed set of four passions, two of which (anger and greed) are the same as the Kural's.
35.source: Dasavaikalika Sutra 8.38-39 (numbering varies by edition), as Saman Suttam vv. 135-136, Samyamasutra (tr. T.K. Tukol and K.K. Dixit; text via jainworld.com)
35._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on jainworld; the four-fault structure and two of its members match, but the Jain list has pride and deceit where the Kural has envy and harsh speech, and the Dasavaikalika verse number differs between editions (8.37-38 or 8.38-39).

36.quote_or_event: “He who can call Death his friend, or who can escape him, or who knows that he will not die, might perhaps decide: this shall be done tomorrow.” … ‘Whenever you die, O king, and leave all pleasant things behind, the Law alone, and nothing else in this world, will save you, O monarch.’
36.explanation: The two young sons of the priest Bhrigu refuse their father's advice to put off renunciation until old age, since no one has a pact with death. Later Queen Kamalavati tells the king that at death dharma alone goes with a person and protects them.
36.tie_back: This covers both halves of the Kural. One should not say 'we will see to it later', and the Law is the one companion that does not perish when the body does.
36.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 14.27 and 14.40 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895)
36._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; a near one-to-one match on both the warning against delay and virtue as the sole protection at death.

37.quote_or_event: “Every good deed will bear its fruit to men; there is no escape from the effect of one's actions.” … “You are now a king of great power and prosperity, enjoying the reward of your good actions”
37.explanation: The brothers Citta and Sambhuta, once born together as outcaste Svapakas, meet in a later life, one as the universal monarch Brahmadatta and the other as a monk. They explain their very different stations as the visible fruit of past karma.
37.tie_back: The Kural points to the gap between the palanquin-bearer and the rider as visible proof of virtue's fruit. The Jain story makes the same point, reading a king's splendour and an outcaste's misery as the open results of past deeds.
37.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 13.1-20, esp. 13.10 and 13.20 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895)
37._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; a strong fit on social station as visible karmic fruit, but the Jain story then subverts it, since the prosperous king clings to pleasure and sinks into hell (13.34), and this carries the same modern caveat about justifying inequality that the Kural's commentators raise.

38.quote_or_event: “The day that goes by will never return; the days elapse without profit to him who acts contrary to the Law. The day that goes by will never return; the days elapse with much profit to him who acts up to the Law.” … “We will even now adopt the Law, after the adoption of which we shall not be born again.”
38.explanation: Bhrigu's sons tell their father that each day spent without dharma is lost for good, while each day spent in it bears fruit, and that by taking up the Law now they will close off future births.
38.tie_back: The Kural's practice of letting no day fall away empty, which becomes a stone blocking the road of rebirth, appears here in almost the same terms. In Jain terms the blocking is samvara, the stopping of karma's inflow.
38.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 14.24-25 and 14.28 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895)
38._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim (Jacobi notes the original reckons by 'nights'); a near one-to-one match on both the unwasted day and the ending of rebirth, though the Kural's road-blocking stone is its own image.

39.quote_or_event: “All singing is but prattle, all dancing is but mocking, all ornaments are but a burden, all pleasures produce but pains. O king, pleasures which the ignorant like, but which produce pains, do not delight pious monks who care not for pleasure, but are intent on the virtues of right conduct.”
39.explanation: The monk Citta tells King Brahmadatta that pleasures pursued for their own sake only end in pain, and that the joy of the wise lies in the virtues of right conduct.
39.tie_back: The Kural says that only what comes through virtue is true pleasure, and that everything else falls outside pleasure altogether. Citta likewise reclassifies sense-pleasure as pain and places real delight in right conduct.
39._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; strong on pleasure outside virtue being pain, but the Kural (per Parimelazhagar) endorses pleasure within domestic virtue, whereas Citta rejects sensual pleasure outright and allows the householder only noble deeds and compassion as a second-best (13.32).

40.quote_or_event: “One should desist from one thing, and practise another: desist from neglect of self-control, and practise self-control.”
40.explanation: The 'Mode of Life' lecture opens by reducing the whole Jain discipline to one twofold rule: turn away from lack of restraint (asamyama) and take up restraint (samyama).
40.tie_back: Like the Kural's closing definition, the Jain rule splits all conduct into what is to be done and what is to be shunned. The Jain criterion is restraint for the soul's sake, where the Kural speaks of public blame (pazhi).
40._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; a close structural match to the do/avoid binary, though the Jain criterion is inner restraint rather than the Kural's socially answerable 'blame'.
